name: Silver
lede: Silver is the color of the moon's metal, shown on screens as a light neutral grey, though the real thing is all reflection: it paid for empires, drew fine Renaissance sketches in silverpoint, stained medieval glass yellow and underlies photography.

sections.title: A metal before a color
sections.body:
Silver is the name of a metal first and a color second. The English word goes back to Old English *seolfor* and a Germanic root whose deeper origin is unknown [30]. Latin called the metal *argentum*, and the Spanish named a whole country after it: Argentina means, in effect, the silvery land [8]. Heraldry kept the Latin, so a silver field on a coat of arms is blazoned argent [11][14].

Dictionaries define the color by the metal. Paterson's entry is simply the lustrous color of the precious metal, with silvery for anything that has its sheen and silver grey for a bluish grey [14]. Language treats it as a thing more than a hue: English happily says reddish or greyish, but there is no silverish, only silvery [14].

Older English sometimes counted silver as white [14]. Paterson records that tribute paid in silver coin was called white mail, as against blackmail paid in grain or cattle [14]. In Devon and Cornwall the dues that tin mines paid in silver were still called white rent until 1838 [14].

sections.title: Money, mines and the moon
sections.body:
Silver has been worked for a very long time. St Clair reports Neolithic silver beads in Egypt and one hoard of 153 silver vessels weighing nearly 20 pounds [8]. When Carthage lost to Rome in 202 BC it paid its war debt in silver, about 360 tons over 50 years [9]. Herodotus, as Birren quotes him, describes a city ringed by seven walls, the last two plated in silver and gold [29].

The metal shaped the early modern world. In January 1545, according to local tradition, a man looking for a lost llama lit a fire on a Bolivian mountain and saw silver run out of the ground beneath it [8]. Cerro Rico de Potosí became one of the two richest mines of the Spanish Empire [8]. Between the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries Spain shipped about 150,000 tons of American silver, around 80 per cent of the world's supply, dug by forced indigenous labor under a version of the Inca *mita* system [8]. Accidents and mercury poisoning were common, and locals called Cerro Rico the mountain that eats men [8].

Silver also had a place in the sky. Gold was paired with the sun and silver with the moon, a match St Clair finds apt because silver waxes and wanes, bright when polished and dark when a film of black silver sulfide forms [8]. In late medieval tables of correspondences, white stood for silver among metals and for the moon among planets [10]. Alchemical imagery cast the pair as a white queen, silver, and a red king, gold [19].

sections.title: Beliefs and legends
sections.body:
Silver gathered stories. A widespread belief held that silver changed color when it touched poison, and St Clair credits that belief with making silver tableware fashionable and then standard [8]. The idea is a belief, not a test: tarnish is the ordinary darkening of the metal described above [8].

The silver bullet is a legend too. St Clair dates its first recorded appearance to the mid-seventeenth century, in a story of students in Greifswald, in northern Germany, casting silver musket balls against werewolves [8]. In the twentieth century the metal turned from the past to the future: it dressed the first American astronauts and, in the 1960s, the metal and foil clothes of the Paris designers Paco Rabanne and André Courrèges [8]. Andy Warhol painted his New York studio silver and used silver and aluminium in his work [24].

sections.title: Silver in art: leaf, point and stain
sections.body:
Painters used real silver in three main ways. The first was as leaf and powder. Silver leaf was common, and in illuminated manuscripts powdered silver could even imitate gold under a yellow glaze of saffron or aloe [15][2]. Byzantine scribes wrote in gold or silver on purple-dyed parchment, and Chinese and Korean Buddhist sutras of the ninth to fifteenth centuries were copied in silver and gold on indigo-dyed paper [27].

Silver also worked hidden beneath other colors. Sassetta laid silver leaf under a transparent crimson glaze to make Saint Francis's robe glow, a trick that only came to light when the panels were examined [16]. Patrons wrote the metal into contracts: a memorandum for Fra Angelico's Linaiuoli Tabernacle asked for gold, blue and silver of the best that could be found, and Piero della Francesca's contract of 1454 also stipulated gold and silver [16].

The second use was drawing. Before graphite pencils spread in Europe in the sixteenth century, artists sketched in silverpoint: a stylus tipped with silver wire, drawn across a ground of chalk or bone ash, which left a fine dark line [6][7]. The third was glass. Around 1300 glaziers developed silver stain, a silver compound painted on glass and fired into it [17][13]. It turned clear glass yellow, blue glass green and red glass orange, which let hair and draperies be painted in the pale yellow typical of fourteenth-century windows [13][17].

In mosaic, silver arrived just after gold. Gage dates the first metallic gold and then silver tesserae to the early third century AD [18]. In Byzantine churches, rays of light around Christ were set in gold and silver, and Gage notes a side effect: when the metal flashes, the colors beside it look least saturated [18].

sections.title: Silver in the paintbox
sections.body:
Most paints called silver contain none. Silver white, or *blanc d'argent* in French, was by George Field's account in 1835 simply a fine lead white [3]. An earlier recipe recorded by de Massoul did use silver, but by the nineteenth century the name only meant brilliant whiteness, as one colorman wrote in 1845 [3][4]. Paterson's dictionary still treats silver-white as a name for white lead [14].

Silver mining fed the paintbox all the same. For three centuries, from the 1400s to the 1700s, painters' usual cheap substitute for costly blues was verditer, a copper blue that came out of silver refining as a by-product [1][23]. Coles passes on an origin story in which a copper solution left over from separating silver was spilled onto chalk, which turned color at once [23]. Late medieval recipes also described a mysterious silver-blue made by exposing silver to vinegar or ammonia fumes; Ball suggests the blue came from copper in the metal, though the recipes insist on pure silver [2].

Other colors came out of the same mines. Cobalt ore turned up in silver workings, and miners blamed its poisonous fumes on goblins called kobolds [23][2]. Litharge, a lead oxide, was another by-product of refining silver, and silver chromate was sold in the nineteenth century as a purple-red artists' color [4].

sections.title: The silver image
sections.body:
Photography is a silver technology. In 1725 the German anatomist Johann Heinrich Schulze showed that certain silver salts darken because of sunlight, not heat [12]. He stenciled letters onto a bottle of chalk and silver nitrate solution, and the words appeared in the liquid where light fell [12].

The dark in an old photograph is metallic silver in tiny grains, which absorb light rather than reflect it [12]. Silver bromide responds most strongly to blue light, so color film needs yellow filter layers to keep blue light away from its red- and green-sensitive layers [12]. In color processing, dyes are built up where silver grains have formed, and the silver is then washed away [12]. So the same metal that looks bright in a spoon looks black in a negative: what changes is the size of the pieces.

sections.title: How painters show silver
sections.body:
A flat swatch cannot show silver, because the metal is about reflection, not hue. Jarman asked whether silver is simply grey, and why gold and silver seem to stand apart from the colors [25]. The Werner chart of 1821 left metallic colors out entirely, on the grounds that they would tarnish on the page and everyone knew them anyway [28].

Painters answered with contrast. Alberti wrote that white and black, used with skill, can represent gold, silver and glass [22]. Jean-Baptiste Oudry told the French Academy in 1749 to paint a silver vase among linen, paper, satin and porcelain, so that the other whites would show what white the silver needed [20]. In Dutch still lifes, the glimmer on a silver jug is a touch of lead white beside dark reflections [7].

Where to look: next time you see a silver spoon or car, notice that almost none of it is mid-grey. It is mostly dark reflections and a few near-white highlights, with the world's colors bent across it. Gertrude Jekyll made the same discovery with plants: her grey garden of silvery leaves, reached through borders of orange, made lilac, lavender and pink flowers look astonishingly luminous [26].

sections.title: Argent
sections.body:
Heraldry gives silver a formal place. European blazon, standard by the sixteenth century, used two metals, or and argent, beside the colors red, blue, green and black [11]. Gage reads the list as a vocabulary of value: two precious metals and costly materials [11].

The heralds' best-known rule is that metal must not sit on metal, nor color on color, which in practice keeps every charge light on dark or dark on light [21]. Pastoureau notes that argent and or were usually painted plain white and yellow; only from the late twelfth century were they sometimes shown in real silver and gold [5]. Real silver tarnished, so painted rolls of arms normally show argent as white [21].

sections.title: The swatch and its relatives
sections.body:
The swatch on this page is the web's `silver`, `#C0C0C0`: a light, perfectly neutral grey [30][31]. It is one of the 140 X11 colors and one of the sixteen basic color names of HTML [14]. A screen can only show it flat, so treat it as the average tone of a silver object, not its look [31].

Its relatives lean in different directions. Crayola's [[silver-crayola|Silver]] is a warmer, faintly pinkish grey, about four and a half units away [31]. [[silver-grey]] and [[roman-silver]] are darker and bluer, [[silver-pink]] is a greyed pink, and [[platinum]] sits a little lighter and warmer [31]. Finlay notes that jewelers once set diamonds in silver because it suited clear stones better than gold, until lighter, stronger platinum took over [32].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Grey this light is common in paintings. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a screen color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 1,127 works, nearly one in twenty [31]. In 95 per cent of them it is the lightest note, a highlight or a pale sky [31]. Its rate doubles in the 1900s, where it appears in one painting in ten [31].

The painters who return to it are painters of weather. Camille Pissarro carries it in 14 of his 50 works here, about six times the archive rate, and Danish painting shows it twice as often as the archive average [31]. The single strongest match is Gustav Klimt's *[[art:commons-Q58427233|Beethoven Frieze]]* of 1901, where a pale grey covers 87 per cent of the photographed panel [31].

These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test: almost none of these greys are silver metal [31]. Real silver leaf in an old painting has often tarnished dark, so it may not match this swatch at all [8]. In Google Books the word *silver* peaks around 1894 and is printed about a quarter as often by 2000 [33].

questions.q: How did painters like Alberti and Oudry make a surface look like silver?
choices: By placing near-white highlights against dark reflections and other whites
By mixing powdered silver into grey paint
By using a special silver-grey pigment
questions.answer: By placing near-white highlights against dark reflections and other whites

questions.q: True or false: the paint sold as silver white was usually made from silver.
What did medieval glaziers' silver stain do to clear glass when fired?

openers: Silver stained medieval glass yellow, not grey: fired into clear glass, a silver compound turns it gold.
Look at a silver spoon: almost none of it is grey. It is dark reflections and a few white highlights.
English once called tribute paid in silver coin white mail, the opposite of blackmail.
